facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a creditor-neutral reading is control without creditor-side visibility. The sponsors hold the voting majority, hold registration rights that allow large sales, are exempted from the anti-takeover provisions, and have waived the corporate opportunity duty, while the refinancing priced the term loan 100 bp wider and the adjusted earnings measure includes a 50% share of a joint venture's EBITDA, 11.3% of the fiscal 2025 total, that is equity accounted rather than consolidated. A debt-funded distribution, a transfer of assets to a non-guarantor subsidiary, a sponsor sell-down that changes control, or fees to sponsors disclosed in the proxy statement would move the view toward higher risk; restricted-payment limits that prove tight in the executed documents, a continued run of voluntary prepayments and sustained positive comparable sales would move it the other way. facts.text: On February 2, 2026, the day after fiscal 2025 closed, the company amended its First Lien Credit Agreement and issued USD 600.0 million of 8.25% senior secured notes due February 1, 2031. It cost USD 28.442 million in cash, of which about USD 20.7 million was capitalised, and it produced a USD 11.84 million loss on extinguishment and modification that includes a non-cash write-off. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against the improving view is that trading has not yet recovered: net sales are flat, supplies and companion animals sales are still falling, the footprint is shrinking, and the profit gain came from cost cuts and a one-off refund while fixed rent absorbs any shortfall. If comparable sales turned negative again, the issuer's fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook of USD 415 million to USD 430 million proved too high, or the revolver could not be extended before 2029, the view would move toward weaker; two further quarters of positive comparable sales with cost savings holding, continued voluntary prepayments and adjusted net leverage reaching the issuer's 2x target would move it toward stronger. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation E20; calculation E21; calculation E30

facts.label: Company description
facts.text: Petco is a United States pet specialty retailer that sold USD 5,961.467 million in fiscal 2025, with consumables at 49.8% of net sales, supplies and companion animals at 33.0% and services and other, mainly veterinary care, grooming and training, at 17.2%, up from 16.3%. It sells through leased pet care centers, an e-commerce site and an app, and sales are substantially all on a cash basis, so receivable risk is small. The credit linkage is that roughly two thirds of sales are consumables and services that recur through the year, which supports cash-flow visibility and debt service, while the shrinking store base, with 16 net closures in fiscal 2025 and 15 to 20 more planned, means the visibility is of a smaller business each year. The 2016 sponsor acquisition, the 2021 listing and the February 2026 refinancing are the history that shapes the capital structure. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 92; calculation E25; calculation E33; EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2

facts.label: Ownership and group structure
facts.text: Two sponsors, CVC funds and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, control the company through Scooby Aggregator, LP, which holds about 65% of the votes, can designate a majority of directors and benefits from controlled-company exemptions, so there is no independent-majority check. The borrower and note issuer is itself a holding company with nominal net worth that operates through an indirect subsidiary, and the guarantors are not named, so structural priority cannot be established even though consolidated figures describe the group. The credit implication is that sponsor-friendly action is limited by the debt documents and not by the board, which the evidence has not let us read; conduct so far has been creditor-aligned, with no dividends, no repurchases and three voluntary prepayments totalling USD 245.25 million. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E24

facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Sales are partly recurring and partly discretionary, and the discretionary part is weakening. Consumables fell 2.5% in fiscal 2025 and were flat in the first half of 2026, supplies and companion animals fell 5.1% and then 2.3%, and services grew 2.6% and then 5.2%, so the mix is shifting toward services, which carry veterinary labour cost but differentiate the offer from online sellers. The issuer attributes the fiscal 2025 sales decline to lower transaction volume and a lower center count, and says competitors have cut prices and forced it to cut prices on some products, so pricing power is limited. No customer concentration is described and no vendor exceeds 10% of sales, so the credit risk is volume and price in a contested market, not concentration. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Margins can be defended against modest volume pressure but not against a repeat of fiscal 2025's sales decline without further cost action. Total lease cost was 9.1% of net sales and operating lease cost alone was 1.30x reported EBITDA, so rent is the largest fixed claim after debt service; selling, general and administrative expense is also largely labour and is exposed to wage inflation and veterinary shortages. Management cut that expense by USD 132.71 million in fiscal 2025 and lifted the gross profit rate from 38.0% to 38.7%, so the cost lever has worked once; the reported EBITDA margin rose from 3.52% in fiscal 2024 to 5.32% in fiscal 2025 and 5.54% over the last twelve months, but part of the first half 2026 gross margin gain is the tariff refund and normalised second quarter gross margin was about flat. facts.label: Capital intensity and free cash flow conversion
facts.text: Free cash flow conversion is solid and capital expenditure is flexible, but the last twelve months flatter it. Capital expenditure was USD 127.097 million in fiscal 2025, 2.1% of net sales, split between about USD 54.06 million for pet care centers, USD 53.572 million for digital and technology and USD 19.465 million for supply chain and other, and down from USD 225.598 million in fiscal 2023 on fewer new centers and hospitals; free cash flow of USD 186.953 million in fiscal 2025 was helped by a USD 63.119 million inventory reduction and the last twelve months by interest paid USD 28.10 million below expense. Operating leases run through operating cash flow, so EBITDA is already after rent, and the fixed charge style cover of 1.36x shows how little room rent and interest leave. facts.label: Porter's five forces
facts.text: Rivalry is the force that matters most. Specialty chains, independent stores, online retailers, supermarkets, warehouse clubs and mass merchants all sell the same consumables, some with more capital, and price cuts by competitors have forced Petco to reduce prices, which caps gross margin and makes comparable sales the key swing factor for leverage. New entrants are a moderate threat, mainly independent stores with distinctive offers and online sellers; substitutes are strong for products, because the same goods can be bought online or at a grocer, and weaker for services, where veterinary care, grooming and training anchor the visit. Buyer power is high because consumers can switch freely and discretionary spending has softened, while supplier power is moderate: the ten largest vendors supplied about 40% of sales, none above 10%, vendors may leave on 90 days' notice, but owned brands carry higher margins and vendor allowances reduce cost of sales. Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, pages 11, 15, 22–23, 108; calculation E33

facts.label: PEST
facts.text: Two factors are material to credit and the others are supportive background. Tariffs are the political factor: the issuer sources from Asia, tariffs and fuel have raised costs before, and a USD 6.8 million net refund flattered the second quarter, so cost pass-through is uncertain and the refund is not a run-rate benefit. Economic conditions matter through softening discretionary spending, which hits supplies and companion animals, and through floating rates on about 59.94% of principal; pet humanization and premiumization and a steady pet population are social tailwinds that support consumables and services, and e-commerce is the technological force that raises price transparency. facts.label: Financial profile and credit quality
facts.text: Scale and market position are Average: the business is large, but market share is not supplied and the footprint is shrinking. Competitive advantage is Average because services, owned brands and an omni-channel offer differentiate it from pure retailers while rivals cut prices. Diversification is Average: three product groups, services and several channels, but one segment and one country, and no customer concentration is described. Cost and capex flexibility is Average because savings were delivered in fiscal 2025 and capital expenditure was cut by USD 98.50 million over two years, yet rent is fixed. Margin stability is Weak, though improving, because reported EBITDA margin moved from 3.52% to 5.32% in a year while sales fell. Free cash flow stability is Weak on history, being negative in fiscal 2023 and USD 49.68 million in fiscal 2024 before USD 186.95 million in fiscal 2025, with timing items in the latest year. Ability to refinance is Average: the February 2026 refinancing extended maturities to 2031 at a higher cost, no ratings are supplied and the revolver must be extended by 2029. Liquidity is Strong at USD 781.1 million with minimal amortisation, subject to covenant terms not seen. Financial policy and governance is Average: conduct is creditor-aligned but control is concentrated and disclosure of covenants and guarantors is not available. The main supports are liquidity, cash generation and policy, the main constraints are leverage, rent and flat sales, the trend is improving, and the missing data are covenant levels, ranking, peer data and pro forma debt. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E01; calculation E19; calculation E29

facts.label: Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds
facts.text: Over the next 12 to 24 months the issuer guides fiscal 2026 net sales flat to up 1.5%, adjusted EBITDA of USD 415 million to USD 430 million, net interest expense of about USD 122 million and capital expenditure of about USD 140 million; those figures imply second-half adjusted EBITDA of USD 195.45 million to USD 210.45 million against USD 204.86 million a year earlier, so the guide assumes flat earnings, not recovery, and any miss reaches leverage quickly. The coupon arithmetic of USD 122.22 million agrees with the interest guide, and the September prepayment saves about USD 6.1 million a year at the term loan rate. Reaching the 2x adjusted target needs USD 333.11 million less net debt at constant adjusted EBITDA, about 1.40 years of last twelve months free cash flow. Over three to five years the revolver must be extended before 2029 and the 2031 balloon refinanced; sector tailwinds are pet humanization and a steady pet population, headwinds are competition, softer discretionary spending, tariffs and wage costs, and company tailwinds are services growth and the membership relaunch against higher interest cost and the loss of the tariff refund. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The realistic downside is a relapse in sales while the membership relaunch and store closures are still working through, on a base where rent is fixed. If net sales fell 2.5% from the last twelve months level, the same fall as in fiscal 2025, the gross profit lost at the fiscal 2025 rate of 38.7% would be about USD 57.72 million; with no cost response, reported EBITDA would fall to USD 272.75 million, net leverage would rise from 3.58x to 4.33x, EBITDA cover of interest expense would fall from 2.55x to 2.10x and cover of run-rate coupons from 2.70x to 2.23x. That is a deliberate upper bound for volume loss, as management cut USD 132.71 million of expense in fiscal 2025 and can cut capital expenditure, and resilience looks sufficient to avoid liquidity distress, because liquidity of USD 781.1 million covers scheduled amortisation many times over and nothing falls due before the revolver in 2029; the financial transmission is to leverage, cover and covenant headroom, not to liquidity, and the observable triggers are comparable sales, the gross profit rate and the revolver extension. Basis: calculation E22; calculation E18; calculation E16; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 92

facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Petco presents an adequate business profile supported by repeat consumables, growing services and a creditor-aligned financial policy, but credit quality is constrained by leverage of 3.58x on reported EBITDA, thin cover after rent and flat sales. Cash-flow durability appears adequate, with free cash flow of USD 237.83 million over the last twelve months, of which USD 28.10 million is interest timing. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on comparable sales holding, the revolver being extended before 2029 and the 2031 balloon being addressed from a lower leverage base. The primary downside path is a sales relapse on the rent-heavy cost base. Further analysis would require the executed debt documents, the lender's EBITDA definition, peer data and a pro forma balance sheet. A comparison with typical leveraged retail issuers is not established because no peer data is supplied. Top risk: a sales relapse on a rent-heavy cost base. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E01; calculation E04; calculation E22

# Source readiness: Petco Health & Wellness Company, Inc. (woof-1826470)
## Request

Source readiness for Petco Health & Wellness Company, Inc. (issuer woof-1826470), as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is whether the six supplied filings and earnings releases support the financial foundation, business and governance, and fundamental credit work, and what is missing. No credit conclusion is drawn.

## Findings
### Bottom line

The six supplied filings and releases are enough to build Petco's financial foundation, business and governance picture and fundamental credit view through the quarter ended August 1, 2026, but not to test covenant headroom or guarantor structure. The issuer is the listed operating company itself, the borrower under the term loan and the asset-based revolver and the issuer of the secured notes, so no parent-versus-subsidiary split is needed, and its sponsors control it from above.

The capital structure changed on February 2, 2026, the day after fiscal 2025 closed. The January 31, 2026 balance sheet still carries the old USD 1,500.0 million term loan, while the August 1, 2026 filing shows USD 897.8 million of term loan and USD 600.0 million of 8.25% secured notes, so the two balance sheets are not like for like. The USD 75.0 million prepayment in September 2026 is a subsequent event, no pro forma balance sheet is supplied, and nothing dated after September 4, 2026 is supplied, so events up to the November 18, 2026 cutoff are not established.

# Financial foundation: Petco Health & Wellness Company, Inc. (woof-1826470)
## Request

Financial foundation for Petco Health & Wellness Company, Inc. (issuer woof-1826470), as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the normalised statements, debt, liquidity, leverage and coverage built from the six supplied filings and releases, with statements in USD thousands and the money tables in USD millions. No credit recommendation is made.
## Sources

## Findings
### Bottom line

Leverage has fallen sharply but is still elevated: net debt is 3.58x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA at August 1, 2026, against 6.58x at fiscal 2024, so creditors depend on the earnings recovery holding rather than on a thick cushion. On issuer-adjusted EBITDA the ratio is 2.78x, but that rests on about USD 94 million of add-backs, chiefly joint venture EBITDA and equity compensation, that cannot be tested against lender definitions.
Basis: calculation C21; calculation C22; calculation C23; calculation C20; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 95; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 22

Liquidity is adequate at USD 781.1 million, and the February 2, 2026 refinancing moved the term loan and the secured notes out to February 2031, but cash interest paid is running below interest expense because of timing, so interest cover of 3.25x on reported EBITDA flatters. The USD 75.0 million prepayment in September 2026 is a subsequent event; no pro forma balance sheet is supplied, so pro forma net debt and leverage are not established.
Basis: calculation C25; calculation C24; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 10–12; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 24; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 11
### Leverage trajectory and drivers

Reported leverage fell because earnings recovered and debt was repaid, not because add-backs grew. Net debt on balance-sheet carrying values went from USD 1,417.681 million at fiscal 2024 to USD 1,236.399 million at fiscal 2025 and USD 1,181.928 million at August 1, 2026, while reported EBITDA rose from USD 215.568 million to USD 317.143 million and USD 330.469 million on a last-twelve-months basis, taking net leverage from 6.58x to 3.90x to 3.58x. The fiscal 2025 gain came from a SG&A reduction of USD 132.7 million (2,184.639 against 2,317.351) on net sales that fell USD 155.0 million, and from a USD 95.25 million voluntary term loan repayment in the fourth quarter; the issuer links the SG&A decrease to lower payroll and consulting costs and improved actuarial results from employee benefits optimisation.

Basis: calculation C16; calculation C06; calculation C21; calculation C22; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 111; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, pages 92–93; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 132

The adjusted measure tells a more favourable story than the reported one because the gap between them is large and moves with items the issuer defines. In fiscal 2025 the gap was USD 91.024 million: equity compensation of USD 32.65 million, USD 46.135 million for 50% of the Mexico joint venture's EBITDA, and USD 12.239 million of other costs; the joint venture is equity accounted, so its EBITDA is not cash the issuer controls.
Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 95; calculation C20
### Coverage and cash interest

Reported EBITDA covered cash interest paid 1.56x in fiscal 2024, 2.54x in fiscal 2025 and 3.25x over the last twelve months, but the last figure is flattered. Interest paid, net, in the 26 weeks to August 1, 2026 was USD 39.419 million against USD 62.441 million a year earlier, while interest expense was USD 65.34 million against USD 66.791 million, and the issuer attributes the stronger operating cash flow partly to the timing of interest and rent payments. The senior secured notes pay semiannually, so the timing of the coupon dates around the quarter end is not established.
Basis: calculation C24; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 24; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 11
### Cash-flow quality

Operating cash flow was USD 314.05 million in fiscal 2025 against USD 177.673 million in fiscal 2024, helped by a USD 63.119 million inventory reduction and partly offset by a USD 42.992 million fall in payables; capital expenditure was USD 127.097 million, leaving free cash flow of USD 186.953 million. In the 26 weeks to August 1, 2026, free cash flow was USD 60.796 million against USD 9.922 million, and the issuer cites timing of interest and rent payments, lower inventory purchases and net tariff refunds, with a USD 6.8 million net tariff benefit inside second quarter results. Operating lease cash costs run through operating cash flow, while finance lease principal of USD 5.614 million in fiscal 2025 sits in financing.
Basis: calculation C33; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 113; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 23–24; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 18
### Liquidity and refinancing

Liquidity at August 1, 2026 was USD 781.1 million, made up of USD 293.498 million of cash and USD 487.6 million of undrawn ABL availability after USD 58.4 million of letters of credit. The February 2, 2026 refinancing replaced the USD 1,500.0 million term loan, due March 2028, with a USD 900.0 million term loan and USD 600.0 million of 8.25% senior secured notes, both due in February 2031, at a loss on extinguishment and modification of USD 11.84 million and USD 28.442 million of cash refinancing costs and original issue discount. The undrawn ABL matures in March 2029, before the term debt, and the annual report says it must be repaid, refinanced or extended before that debt matures; no facility matures within twelve months of that date, and term loan amortisation is USD 9.0 million a year, so almost all principal falls due in 2031.

Basis: calculation C25; calculation C27; calculation C28; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 10–12; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 70
### Subsequent events and multi-figure items

Two events fall after the balance-sheet dates and are kept out of period figures. The February 2, 2026 refinancing falls one day after the fiscal 2025 year-end, so the January 31, 2026 balance sheet still shows the old term loan; the USD 75.0 million voluntary prepayment of the term loan in September 2026 falls after the August 1, 2026 balance sheet. Neither has a pro forma balance sheet in the sources, so pro forma net debt and leverage are not established.
Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 133; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 11; EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2

The refinancing costs appear as three different figures for different purposes: a loss on extinguishment and modification of USD 11.84 million in the income statement, USD 28.442 million of refinancing costs and original issue discount paid in cash, and about USD 20.7 million of costs capitalised against the new debt (USD 1.4 million on the term loan, USD 9.0 million of original issue discount and USD 10.3 million on the notes). The cash figure serves net debt and liquidity, the expense figure serves earnings, and the capitalised figure explains the gap between principal and carrying value.
### Definition and data-quality risks

The issuer's own net debt includes all finance leases, so it differs from the carrying-value measure used here by the non-current finance leases that sit in other long-term liabilities: USD 4.481 million at August 1, 2026. Adjusted EBITDA is described by the issuer as calculated differently under its debt agreements, and the lender definition and the covenant levels are not in the sources, so no covenant capacity is stated. Cash and equivalents at August 1, 2026 exclude restricted cash of USD 1.004 million, while the cash flow statement's cash includes it.
Basis: calculation C34; EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 9

## Findings
### Bottom line

Petco is a sponsor-controlled, lease-heavy pet retailer whose documented financial policy has been neutral to supportive for creditors, but the protections that matter to them sit in debt documents and a proxy statement that are not in the evidence. The sponsors hold about 65% of the votes through one holding vehicle, the company pays no dividends and has repurchased no shares, and it has prepaid USD 245.3 million of term loan voluntarily since fiscal 2023, so no extraction is documented.
Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 70; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 85; calculation D05

Operating risk matters more than control: comparable sales fell 1.6% in fiscal 2025 and stores keep closing, on a base where total lease cost is 9.1% of net sales. Fund life, sponsor economics and related-party fees are not disclosed, so exit pressure and fee leakage are not established.
Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 92; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 128; EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation D04
### Key findings

- Demand is mostly consumables and services, about 67% of net sales, with no customer concentration described, and vendor dependence is moderate. Consumables were 49.8% of fiscal 2025 net sales and services and other 17.2%, up from 16.3%, while the ten largest vendors supplied about 40% of sales and none exceeded 10%; sales to customers are substantially all on a cash basis, so receivable and customer-credit risk is small, but vendor terms and allowances drive working capital and cost of sales, and the auditor names vendor allowances as a critical audit matter.

Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 92; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 98; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 108; calculation D01; calculation D08

- Rent is the largest fixed claim and makes earnings sensitive to sales. Total lease cost was USD 542.55 million in fiscal 2025, 9.1% of net sales, across a pet care center base that is almost entirely leased and every distribution center, so a small sales fall compresses margins unless costs fall with it; the company has net closed stores, plans 15 to 20 more net closures in fiscal 2026, and cut selling, general and administrative expense to 36.6% of net sales in fiscal 2025.

Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 128; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 85; EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 92; calculation D04

- Sponsors control the company without an independent-majority check. The principal stockholder controls about 65% of the votes, sponsors can designate a majority of directors, four of ten directors are affiliated with them, the company uses every controlled-company exemption, and the corporate opportunity duty is waived; the creditor consequence is that sponsor-friendly actions are constrained by the debt documents and the dividend policy rather than by board independence, and those documents are not supplied.

- Documented behaviour is creditor-neutral to supportive, and no extraction is evidenced. The company has paid no dividends, repurchased no shares and prepaid term loan principal of USD 75.0 million in fiscal 2023, USD 95.3 million in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025 and USD 75.0 million in September 2026, and the February 2026 refinancing pushed maturities out to 2031 at a higher cost, with the term loan's weighted average rate at 8.1% on 2026-08-01 against 7.3% on 2026-01-31.

Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 85; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 132; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation D05

- The borrower and note issuer is a holding company, so creditors depend on subsidiary guarantees. The annual report says the company and certain subsidiaries are holding companies with nominal net worth that conduct business through an indirect operating subsidiary, Petco Animal Supplies Stores, Inc., and the guarantors are not named. This corrects the earlier source readiness description of the issuer as the operating company itself; the consolidated statements remain the right perimeter for debt, earnings and liquidity, but structural priority is not established.
Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, pages 74–75; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 150; Source readiness (CP-0)

- Trading has stabilised rather than recovered. Comparable sales turned positive at 0.6% in the 26 weeks of 2026 after a 1.3% fall a year earlier, but net sales rose only 0.1%, and the second quarter carried a USD 6.8 million net tariff refund benefit and a sales disruption from the membership relaunch, so the profit gain rests on cost and margin rather than growth.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 18–20; EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation D12
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a creditor-neutral reading is control without creditor-side visibility. The sponsors hold the voting majority, hold registration rights that allow large sales, are exempted from the anti-takeover provisions, and have waived the corporate opportunity duty, while the refinancing priced the term loan 100 bp wider and the adjusted earnings measure includes a 50% share of a joint venture's EBITDA, 11.3% of the fiscal 2025 total, that is equity accounted rather than consolidated. A debt-funded distribution, a transfer of assets to a non-guarantor subsidiary, a sponsor sell-down that changes control, or fees to sponsors disclosed in the proxy statement would move the view toward higher risk; restricted-payment limits that prove tight in the executed documents, a continued run of voluntary prepayments and sustained positive comparable sales would move it the other way.

Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, pages 72–74; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 79; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, pages 95, 132; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 10; calculation D09
### Limitations

- The executed credit agreements and indenture are not supplied, so the capacity of the company and sponsors to pay distributions, move assets or add debt is not established; this limits the behaviour conclusion to what was done, not what is permitted.

- The proxy statement is not supplied, so sponsor fees, related-party transactions, director independence by name and executive pay are not established; the governance view rests on the risk-factor description of control.
- Sponsor fund vintage, remaining fund life, entry price and economic ownership are not disclosed, so no exit-pressure or sell-down inference is drawn.

- The earlier source readiness description of the issuer as the operating company is corrected by the annual report's holding-company statement; guarantor identities and structural priority remain open.
- Nothing dated after September 4, 2026 is supplied, so sponsor actions or financings between that date and the cutoff are not established.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

On February 2, 2026, the day after fiscal 2025 closed, the company amended its First Lien Credit Agreement and issued USD 600.0 million of 8.25% senior secured notes due February 1, 2031. New term loans of USD 900.0 million, due February 2, 2031 and priced at Term SOFR plus 4.25%, together with the notes and cash on hand, repaid the USD 1,500.0 million term loan that was due in March 2028 and priced 100 bp lower. The refinancing removed the 2028 maturity. It cost USD 28.442 million in cash, of which about USD 20.7 million was capitalised, and it produced a USD 11.84 million loss on extinguishment and modification that includes a non-cash write-off. The new borrowings of USD 1,500.0 million equalled the principal repaid, so it raised no new money, and no sponsor equity is described.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 6, 8; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, pages 100, 133; calculation D10

The notes may be redeemed at a make-whole price before February 1, 2028 and at prices set in the indenture afterwards, and a change of control may trigger redemption; the indenture restricts additional debt, distributions, asset sales, liens and affiliate transactions subject to exceptions that are not supplied. The asset-based revolver was undrawn at 2026-08-01 with USD 546.0 million of commitments maturing on March 29, 2029, after a March 2024 amendment extended most of it, and its first USD 35.0 million tranche matured on March 4, 2026. The credit agreements name covenants on debt, liens, fundamental changes, investments and restricted payments and, for the revolver, a fixed charge coverage ratio, and the company reports compliance at 2026-08-01; the levels are not supplied.

In September 2026, after the second quarter closed, the company prepaid USD 75.0 million of the term loan from cash on hand, applied to scheduled payments in order of date; this subsequent event is not in any period figure of this module and no new debt issue is recorded after February 2, 2026.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 11; EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2

# Fundamental credit: Petco Health & Wellness Company, Inc. (woof-1826470)
## Request

Fundamental credit synthesis for Petco Health & Wellness Company, Inc. (issuer woof-1826470), as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the integrated business and financial credit view built on the six supplied filings and releases and the three earlier modules; no rating, legal-capacity, recovery, relative-value or sizing conclusion is drawn.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Petco's credit is improving but still leveraged: cost cuts lifted reported earnings and cut net debt to 3.58x EBITDA, and liquidity of USD 781.1 million with maturities pushed to 2031 buys time, yet flat sales leave the recovery unproven.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation E01; calculation E03

Coverage is thinner than the headline suggests, with EBITDA covering interest expense 2.55x and EBITDA before rent covering rent plus cash interest 1.36x, and the documents that would show covenant room and ranking are not in the evidence. The primary downside is a sales relapse on a rent-heavy cost base, which the scenario below puts at 4.33x net leverage before any cost response.
Basis: calculation E07; calculation E12; calculation E22
### Key findings

- Leverage is falling for the right reasons but remains the main constraint. Net debt over reported EBITDA fell from 6.58x at fiscal 2024 to 3.90x at fiscal 2025 and 3.58x over the twelve months to August 1, 2026, because earnings recovered and free cash flow was kept rather than distributed, not because add-backs grew; on the issuer's adjusted EBITDA the ratio is 2.78x, but that rests on about USD 94 million of add-backs that cannot be tested against the lender's definition. Net debt and leverage after the February 2026 refinancing and the September 2026 prepayment are not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation E01; calculation E02

- Coverage is adequate on cash paid but only moderate on any steadier measure. EBITDA covered cash interest 3.25x over the last twelve months, yet cash interest ran USD 28.10 million below interest expense because of payment timing, so cover on interest expense is 2.55x and on the run-rate coupons of the new debt 2.70x; after rent, EBITDA plus rent covered rent plus cash interest only 1.36x in fiscal 2025.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation E05; calculation E06; calculation E07; calculation E08; calculation E10; calculation E11; calculation E12

- Cash generation is the strongest support, but part of it is timing. Free cash flow was USD 186.95 million in fiscal 2025 and USD 237.83 million over the last twelve months, equal to 16.12% of total debt; removing the interest timing gap leaves USD 209.73 million, still enough to take net debt to the issuer's 2x adjusted target in about 1.59 years at constant adjusted EBITDA.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation E04; calculation E09; calculation E21

- Liquidity and the maturity profile are the main protection. Liquidity of USD 781.1 million covers the USD 40.50 million of scheduled term loan payments to 2030 by 19.29x, and 97.30% of principal falls due in 2031, but the undrawn revolver matures in March 2029, ahead of the term debt, and the covenant terms that govern access to it are not supplied.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation E03; calculation E15; calculation E16

- The operating recovery rests on cost cuts, not growth. Selling, general and administrative expense fell USD 132.71 million in fiscal 2025 against a USD 155.0 million fall in net sales, and comparable sales turned from a 1.6% decline to a 0.6% gain in the first half of 2026, but net sales rose only 0.1% and the second quarter included a USD 6.8 million net tariff refund, without which the issuer puts second quarter adjusted EBITDA at USD 115.4 million.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E18; calculation E27; calculation E28

- Rent makes the cost base rigid and earnings sensitive to sales. Operating lease cost was 1.30x reported EBITDA in fiscal 2025 and total lease cost was 9.1% of net sales, so a modest sales fall compresses margin unless costs fall with it; cost and capex flexibility is real but already used, since capital expenditure fell USD 98.50 million between fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2025 and is expected to rise to about USD 140 million in fiscal 2026.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E14; calculation E19; calculation E30; EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2

- Financial policy is creditor-aligned, but control and structure limit what can be assumed. The company pays no dividends and has prepaid USD 245.25 million of term loan since fiscal 2023, yet the sponsors control about 65% of the votes, the borrower is a holding company with unnamed guarantors, and the lender's definition of EBITDA, the covenant levels and the ranking of the debt are not supplied.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation E24; calculation E32

- Interest cost is rising even as debt falls. The term loan's weighted average rate was 8.1% on August 1, 2026 against 7.3% on January 31, 2026, about 59.94% of principal is floating, and 100 bp on the floating term loan would cost USD 8.98 million a year before any hedge, whose terms are not supplied.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation E17; calculation E31
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against the improving view is that trading has not yet recovered: net sales are flat, supplies and companion animals sales are still falling, the footprint is shrinking, and the profit gain came from cost cuts and a one-off refund while fixed rent absorbs any shortfall. If comparable sales turned negative again, the issuer's fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook of USD 415 million to USD 430 million proved too high, or the revolver could not be extended before 2029, the view would move toward weaker; two further quarters of positive comparable sales with cost savings holding, continued voluntary prepayments and adjusted net leverage reaching the issuer's 2x target would move it toward stronger.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation E20; calculation E21; calculation E30
### Limitations

- No peer, market-share or industry-growth data is supplied, so the judgements on scale, competitive advantage and diversification rest on the issuer's own account of its markets; this limits how firmly the Average ratings on those dimensions can be held, not the leverage or cover figures.

- The downside scenario applies one illustrative sales decline at the reported gross profit rate with no cost response; it shows the direction and rough size of the pressure on leverage and cover, not a forecast of either.

- The fixed charge style cover and lease-adjusted leverage are the analyst's own definitions built from reported lease cost and lease liabilities; they are not the lender's definitions and must not be read as covenant capacity.
- Run-rate interest uses a weighted average rate printed to one decimal and ignores hedges whose terms are not supplied, so the interest sensitivity could be overstated or understated.
- The view stops at the second quarter 2026 report and release; the September 2026 prepayment is reflected only as a stated event, and trading since then is not known.
### Strengths and weaknesses

The main strengths are recovering earnings and falling leverage, liquidity of USD 781.1 million with almost all principal due in 2031, repeat consumables and growing services at about two thirds of sales, a financial policy that has favoured creditors, and demonstrated cost and capital expenditure flexibility. The main weaknesses are leverage that is still elevated with thin cover after rent, flat sales in a shrinking footprint, a rent-heavy fixed cost base, earnings that lean on issuer add-backs and one-off items, and sponsor control with unnamed guarantors and unseen covenants.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E03; calculation E12; calculation E15
### Company description

Petco is a United States pet specialty retailer that sold USD 5,961.467 million in fiscal 2025, with consumables at 49.8% of net sales, supplies and companion animals at 33.0% and services and other, mainly veterinary care, grooming and training, at 17.2%, up from 16.3%. It sells through leased pet care centers, an e-commerce site and an app, and sales are substantially all on a cash basis, so receivable risk is small. The credit linkage is that roughly two thirds of sales are consumables and services that recur through the year, which supports cash-flow visibility and debt service, while the shrinking store base, with 16 net closures in fiscal 2025 and 15 to 20 more planned, means the visibility is of a smaller business each year. The 2016 sponsor acquisition, the 2021 listing and the February 2026 refinancing are the history that shapes the capital structure.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 92; calculation E25; calculation E33; EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2
### Ownership and group structure

Two sponsors, CVC funds and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, control the company through Scooby Aggregator, LP, which holds about 65% of the votes, can designate a majority of directors and benefits from controlled-company exemptions, so there is no independent-majority check. The borrower and note issuer is itself a holding company with nominal net worth that operates through an indirect subsidiary, and the guarantors are not named, so structural priority cannot be established even though consolidated figures describe the group. The credit implication is that sponsor-friendly action is limited by the debt documents and not by the board, which the evidence has not let us read; conduct so far has been creditor-aligned, with no dividends, no repurchases and three voluntary prepayments totalling USD 245.25 million.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E24
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Sales are partly recurring and partly discretionary, and the discretionary part is weakening. Consumables fell 2.5% in fiscal 2025 and were flat in the first half of 2026, supplies and companion animals fell 5.1% and then 2.3%, and services grew 2.6% and then 5.2%, so the mix is shifting toward services, which carry veterinary labour cost but differentiate the offer from online sellers. The issuer attributes the fiscal 2025 sales decline to lower transaction volume and a lower center count, and says competitors have cut prices and forced it to cut prices on some products, so pricing power is limited. No customer concentration is described and no vendor exceeds 10% of sales, so the credit risk is volume and price in a contested market, not concentration.

Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 92; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 19; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E26
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Margins can be defended against modest volume pressure but not against a repeat of fiscal 2025's sales decline without further cost action. Total lease cost was 9.1% of net sales and operating lease cost alone was 1.30x reported EBITDA, so rent is the largest fixed claim after debt service; selling, general and administrative expense is also largely labour and is exposed to wage inflation and veterinary shortages. Management cut that expense by USD 132.71 million in fiscal 2025 and lifted the gross profit rate from 38.0% to 38.7%, so the cost lever has worked once; the reported EBITDA margin rose from 3.52% in fiscal 2024 to 5.32% in fiscal 2025 and 5.54% over the last twelve months, but part of the first half 2026 gross margin gain is the tariff refund and normalised second quarter gross margin was about flat.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, pages 24, 41; EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation E14; calculation E18; calculation E29
### Capital intensity and free cash flow conversion

Free cash flow conversion is solid and capital expenditure is flexible, but the last twelve months flatter it. Capital expenditure was USD 127.097 million in fiscal 2025, 2.1% of net sales, split between about USD 54.06 million for pet care centers, USD 53.572 million for digital and technology and USD 19.465 million for supply chain and other, and down from USD 225.598 million in fiscal 2023 on fewer new centers and hospitals; free cash flow of USD 186.953 million in fiscal 2025 was helped by a USD 63.119 million inventory reduction and the last twelve months by interest paid USD 28.10 million below expense. Operating leases run through operating cash flow, so EBITDA is already after rent, and the fixed charge style cover of 1.36x shows how little room rent and interest leave.
Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, pages 98–99; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation E04; calculation E06; calculation E08; calculation E12; calculation E19
### Porter's five forces

Rivalry is the force that matters most. Specialty chains, independent stores, online retailers, supermarkets, warehouse clubs and mass merchants all sell the same consumables, some with more capital, and price cuts by competitors have forced Petco to reduce prices, which caps gross margin and makes comparable sales the key swing factor for leverage. New entrants are a moderate threat, mainly independent stores with distinctive offers and online sellers; substitutes are strong for products, because the same goods can be bought online or at a grocer, and weaker for services, where veterinary care, grooming and training anchor the visit. Buyer power is high because consumers can switch freely and discretionary spending has softened, while supplier power is moderate: the ten largest vendors supplied about 40% of sales, none above 10%, vendors may leave on 90 days' notice, but owned brands carry higher margins and vendor allowances reduce cost of sales.
Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, pages 11, 15, 22–23, 108; calculation E33
### PEST

Two factors are material to credit and the others are supportive background. Tariffs are the political factor: the issuer sources from Asia, tariffs and fuel have raised costs before, and a USD 6.8 million net refund flattered the second quarter, so cost pass-through is uncertain and the refund is not a run-rate benefit. Economic conditions matter through softening discretionary spending, which hits supplies and companion animals, and through floating rates on about 59.94% of principal; pet humanization and premiumization and a steady pet population are social tailwinds that support consumables and services, and e-commerce is the technological force that raises price transparency.
Basis: 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, pages 11, 29, 36; 10-Q_2026-08-01_woof-20260801.htm.jsonl, page 20; calculation E17; calculation E27
### SWOT

- Strengths: repeat consumables and growing services; liquidity of USD 781.1 million; creditor-aligned financial policy; cost and capital expenditure flexibility; free cash flow of USD 237.83 million over the last twelve months.

- Weaknesses: leverage of 3.58x on reported EBITDA with thin cover after rent; a rent-heavy, labour-heavy fixed cost base; flat sales and a shrinking footprint; earnings that lean on issuer add-backs; sponsor control and unnamed guarantors.

- Opportunities that could improve credit: services growth, a membership relaunch that lifts repeat visits, owned brands with higher margins, and prepayments that reach the 2x adjusted leverage target.
- Threats that could weaken credit: a renewed fall in comparable sales, competitor price cuts, tariff and wage costs, a failure to extend the revolver before 2029, and sponsor action funded by debt.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E03; calculation E04
### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and market position are Average: the business is large, but market share is not supplied and the footprint is shrinking. Competitive advantage is Average because services, owned brands and an omni-channel offer differentiate it from pure retailers while rivals cut prices. Diversification is Average: three product groups, services and several channels, but one segment and one country, and no customer concentration is described. Cost and capex flexibility is Average because savings were delivered in fiscal 2025 and capital expenditure was cut by USD 98.50 million over two years, yet rent is fixed. Margin stability is Weak, though improving, because reported EBITDA margin moved from 3.52% to 5.32% in a year while sales fell. Free cash flow stability is Weak on history, being negative in fiscal 2023 and USD 49.68 million in fiscal 2024 before USD 186.95 million in fiscal 2025, with timing items in the latest year. Ability to refinance is Average: the February 2026 refinancing extended maturities to 2031 at a higher cost, no ratings are supplied and the revolver must be extended by 2029. Liquidity is Strong at USD 781.1 million with minimal amortisation, subject to covenant terms not seen. Financial policy and governance is Average: conduct is creditor-aligned but control is concentrated and disclosure of covenants and guarantors is not available. The main supports are liquidity, cash generation and policy, the main constraints are leverage, rent and flat sales, the trend is improving, and the missing data are covenant levels, ranking, peer data and pro forma debt.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E01; calculation E19; calculation E29
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the issuer guides fiscal 2026 net sales flat to up 1.5%, adjusted EBITDA of USD 415 million to USD 430 million, net interest expense of about USD 122 million and capital expenditure of about USD 140 million; those figures imply second-half adjusted EBITDA of USD 195.45 million to USD 210.45 million against USD 204.86 million a year earlier, so the guide assumes flat earnings, not recovery, and any miss reaches leverage quickly. The coupon arithmetic of USD 122.22 million agrees with the interest guide, and the September prepayment saves about USD 6.1 million a year at the term loan rate. Reaching the 2x adjusted target needs USD 333.11 million less net debt at constant adjusted EBITDA, about 1.40 years of last twelve months free cash flow. Over three to five years the revolver must be extended before 2029 and the 2031 balloon refinanced; sector tailwinds are pet humanization and a steady pet population, headwinds are competition, softer discretionary spending, tariffs and wage costs, and company tailwinds are services growth and the membership relaunch against higher interest cost and the loss of the tariff refund.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-09-02_woof-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation E10; calculation E20; calculation E21; calculation E23
### Downside scenario

The realistic downside is a relapse in sales while the membership relaunch and store closures are still working through, on a base where rent is fixed. If net sales fell 2.5% from the last twelve months level, the same fall as in fiscal 2025, the gross profit lost at the fiscal 2025 rate of 38.7% would be about USD 57.72 million; with no cost response, reported EBITDA would fall to USD 272.75 million, net leverage would rise from 3.58x to 4.33x, EBITDA cover of interest expense would fall from 2.55x to 2.10x and cover of run-rate coupons from 2.70x to 2.23x. That is a deliberate upper bound for volume loss, as management cut USD 132.71 million of expense in fiscal 2025 and can cut capital expenditure, and resilience looks sufficient to avoid liquidity distress, because liquidity of USD 781.1 million covers scheduled amortisation many times over and nothing falls due before the revolver in 2029; the financial transmission is to leverage, cover and covenant headroom, not to liquidity, and the observable triggers are comparable sales, the gross profit rate and the revolver extension.
Basis: calculation E22; calculation E18; calculation E16; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2026-01-31_woof-20260131.htm.jsonl, page 92
### Overall credit view

Overall, Petco presents an adequate business profile supported by repeat consumables, growing services and a creditor-aligned financial policy, but credit quality is constrained by leverage of 3.58x on reported EBITDA, thin cover after rent and flat sales. Cash-flow durability appears adequate, with free cash flow of USD 237.83 million over the last twelve months, of which USD 28.10 million is interest timing. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on comparable sales holding, the revolver being extended before 2029 and the 2031 balloon being addressed from a lower leverage base. The primary downside path is a sales relapse on the rent-heavy cost base. Further analysis would require the executed debt documents, the lender's EBITDA definition, peer data and a pro forma balance sheet. A comparison with typical leveraged retail issuers is not established because no peer data is supplied. Top risk: a sales relapse on a rent-heavy cost base.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation E01; calculation E04; calculation E22

## Gaps

- Peer, market-share and industry-growth data are not supplied, so scale, competitive advantage and diversification are judged from the issuer's own description and the Average ratings are not benchmarked. Severity Medium. Action: obtain a peer set and industry data.

- Covenant levels, the lender's EBITDA definition, the ranking of the term loan, notes and revolver, and the guarantor list are not supplied, so headroom, structural priority and recovery cannot be assessed in this module. Severity Medium. Action: obtain the executed credit agreements and indenture.

- No pro forma net debt or leverage is supplied for the February 2, 2026 refinancing or the September 2026 prepayment, so those events stay outside the period figures. Severity Medium. Action: obtain a pro forma presentation or the next quarterly report.
- Hedge terms are not supplied, so the interest sensitivity and run-rate coupon cost are computed before hedges. Severity Low. Action: obtain the derivative confirmations.

- Whether the lower first-half cash interest reflects only coupon timing is not established, so the USD 28.10 million timing gap is an estimate. Severity Low. Action: obtain the indenture coupon dates or the third quarter report.

- Comparable sales are not split into traffic and ticket, and the membership relaunch effect is described but not quantified, so the drivers of the first-half 2026 recovery cannot be attributed. Severity Low. Action: obtain management disclosure on traffic and membership.

- The earlier source readiness description of the issuer as the operating company is corrected by the annual report and by the Business & governance module: the company is a holding company. The USD 95.3 million and USD 245.3 million shown there are roundings of the exact USD 95.25 million and USD 245.25 million used here. Severity Low. Action: none beyond the labels.
- No rating or market price is supplied, so the view does not test agency opinion or market-implied risk. Severity Low. Action: supply current ratings if wanted.
